results.question: Why do builders in Veridia care so much whether ordinary people like the look of their buildings?
results.answer_as_shown: Builders care because the public’s aesthetic rating directly determines the “public aesthetics tax,” a major part of the composite land tax they must pay; a higher rating lowers the tax, making their projects more profitable. Thus pleasing ordinary people isn’t just about prestige—it directly impacts developers’ bottom line. [c1-b20]

results.question: When people rate buildings on that minus-five to five slider, why doesn't it help to just give everything extreme scores?
results.answer_as_shown: Because the voting uses quadratic voting, the system automatically rescales all votes so the overall average is zero and the average of the squares equals one. If everyone voted the maximum (+5 or –5), the normalization would compress those extremes, removing any extra influence and making the votes no stronger than a moderate, properly‑weighted vote. Thus the mathematically optimal strategy is to choose the correct direction and a strength that matches how strongly you feel, not to push every slider to the extreme. [c1-b32]

results.question: How do the cities in the United Cities get a say in each other's governments?
results.answer_as_shown: When two United Cities are linked by a co‑governance pact, each city elects a slice of the other’s parliament. The share is set in advance: the larger city (measured by the geometric average of population and GDP) appoints that agreed‑upon percentage of seats in the smaller city’s legislature, while the smaller city appoints a percentage equal to the agreed share divided by the square‑root of the size‑ratio between them [c5-b47][c5-b48]. The square‑root adjustment is explained as reflecting the super‑linear utility a larger participant gets from holding a big share of governance [c5-b49].

Thus, the priests see language as a safe, high‑impact arena compared to the more confrontational or costly domains of economics or defense.

results.question: How can an ordinary buyer be sure their chip comes from the same supply the inspectors test?
results.answer_as_shown: An ordinary buyer can be sure their chip comes from the same pool that inspectors test by purchasing through the mixnet delivery system. In that system only the final node knows the buyer’s address, while the sender and intermediate nodes cannot link a specific chip to a specific recipient. Inspectors also obtain chips via the same mixnet, so the manufacturer cannot give a “clean” chip only to inspectors without also sending it to any buyer who uses the mixnet. Because the mixnet randomizes and hides the destination, the buyer’s chip is drawn from the same random pool that the inspectors examine[c9-b122][c9-b124].

results.question: How does Veridia tax buildings with stuffy indoor air?
results.answer_as_shown: Veridia treats indoor‑air quality as a component of the land tax. If a building’s occupied spaces have perfect air the tax is zero, but when the average reading exceeds about 1,000 (e.g., high CO₂) the building is charged an extra 0.33 % of its land value each year – roughly a sixth of its revenue – with the rate lowered if the building uses filters or UVC. [c11-b98][c11-b99][c11-b100]

results.question: How can a foreigner like Deluin pick up the Dzegojan language so fast?
results.answer_as_shown: Deluin can learn Dzegoban quickly because the language is deliberately limited and visual. It has only 256 roots, so the core vocabulary can be memorized in under a month, letting speakers get by without mastering every nuance[c14-b118]. Version 9 even makes the script more pictographic—hieroglyph‑like symbols for roots with clear pronunciation markers—so the writing doubles as a visual cue to meaning and grammar【c14-b114‑c14-b117】. This systematic, math‑like structure and the small, fixed set of building blocks let a motivated outsider pick up functional use fast.

results.question: How does Gladias's voting setup stop Delwart from checking which way he voted?
results.answer_as_shown: Gladias’s system ties each vote to a cryptographic key that can only be created by physically meeting ≥ 3 members of his Key Allocation Group (KAG) and registering blinded shares of that key with them. Those shares are later combined inside an obfuscated circuit that can decrypt only the final tally—not which individual keys are valid or which vote they correspond to. Because the circuit never reveals the mapping between a voter’s key and the ballot, Delwart cannot tell whether any particular vote is “real” or “fake.” To hijack a vote he would have to impersonate Gladias in person and infiltrate the KAG, which the protocol makes deliberately difficult. [c15-b40][c15-b41]

results.question: What happened when the Arctics took over Redshire?
results.answer_as_shown: The Arctic Empire launched a coordinated strike that instantly overran Redshire. Drones and aircraft landed across cities and bases at the same moment a massive ground force poured out of previously unseen underground tunnels from the north. The Redshire military was caught off‑guard—suspected corruption left it unprepared—so battles lasted under two longhours with few casualties before almost every garrison surrendered. Three government planes carrying the president, prime minister and most of parliament tried to flee but were shot down, with no survivors, and the president’s son was taken captive. The last southern garrison negotiated a conditional surrender, allowing a small group of staff and two senators to fly to Devanvil; all other movements were blocked as the Arctic set up communications jamming and sealed the borders[c15-b6][c15-b8][c15-b10][c15-b12].

results.question: How did Zei work out his opening setup when the game was suddenly played on hexagons?
results.answer_as_shown: Zei first flooded his sandbox with random junk to see what survived or turned into gliders on the new hex grid. Within a minute he spotted a few stable pieces and fast‑moving gliders (which happened to fly directly east) and noted that flipping or rotating them by 60° didn’t work. He then observed that each tick split the board into triangles that rotated the hexes (clockwise with one filled hex, counter‑clockwise with two) and deduced a “cheat‑code” of forward steps and time‑shifts to reverse moves. Using that insight, he quickly placed symbols, walls and gliders that would create the needed symbols when they hit rocks, completing his opening setup.[c12-b152][c12-b169][c12-b170][c12-b181]
